title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
What an honor to emcee the first day of @aiDotEngineer and introduce the Software Factories Track
Thank you @swyx & team, and @KeycardLabs for the support.
“A year ago @GeoffreyHuntley released the Ralph loop. It captured our attention and sparked our imagination as we watched Ralph loops work autonomously overnight and forge entire products on its own.
However, it wasn't perfect and in the early days it came recommended for greenfield work only and it came with the expectation that it would get you about 90% of the way there.
Since then we've learned quite a lot about loop engineering and in the last year there's been considerable advancements that make now that largest inflection point for software factories.
Model vision has improved allowing them to see and verify work they couldn't before. Agents now have access to far richer tool ecosystems and live data, enabling them to work across real production environments. AI security practices have matured, giving agents the security, autonomy, and capability they need to perform meaningful work. Context windows have gotten larger and agent memory has improved allowing agents in a loop to track what's been done before. Lastly, reasoning models have improved helping the model think through more sophisticated tasks.
All of this comes together now.
Software factories are no longer a vision for the future. They've become a practical reality.
Today's speakers are on the frontier of this shift and helping define this inflection point. They'll help us separate what's real from what's hype, share what actually works, and how to build software factories that produce reliable results, not slop.”

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Awesome to see that my talk at @aiDotEngineer has created interest in this direction.
The natural SERP for agents is a workspace created by retrieving candidate documents and allowing the agent to interact with it through familiar tools.
Quoting @johnsonshi86
Came across DR-DCI via @jobergum's talk at @aiDotEngineer. It's tackling a problem that comes up constantly once you're building agents: how does an agent actually search over a large and distributed set of documents.
Traditional RAG has known limits. It chunks documents, embeds them, and hands the agent a handful of disconnected snippets. If the answer got split across a chunk boundary, or needs cross-referencing two documents, the agent has no way to go look further, it only gets the one retrieval pass.
The other extreme, the current "grep is all you need" trend, just gives the agent shell tools and lets it search the raw corpus directly. That's more flexible, but it doesn't hold up at scale, full-corpus grep gets slow and starts timing out as the collection grows across distributed physical nodes.
DR-DCI (paper by @zhuofengli96475 and team) is a hybrid of the two. BM25 runs first and narrows a huge corpus down to a manageable set of candidate documents. Those relevant docs get pulled into a bounded, sandboxed workspace, and only then does the agent run real grep/cat/find against that smaller set instead of the whole corpus. 71% accuracy vs 63% for raw grep-everything, and about 20x faster.
I made some observations of my own on top of the paper, mainly around productionizing this for distributed systems. These include shard locality, tiered caching, caching differences for immutable vs mutable content, fast sandbox setup/teardown for the VFS workspace, and precomputing common queries.
This area (RAG + grep hybrids) feels like a real harness engineering lever for inference providers to differentiate on, both on tool-calling benchmarks and in how agents actually perform on real work.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Eli Cohen from Snyk closed out his talk at @aidotengineer and here's the one thing he hoped the room would take away:
Point-in-time pentesting was built for a world where code changed slowly, and humans did the reasoning.
That world is gone.
AI is writing more code than ever (much of it insecure), and attackers are running the same models - continuously.
If you pentest once a year, what's happening the other 350 days?
The gap isn't in finding more bugs. It's proving the ones that matter, on every change, with the business logic
reasoning that only humans could do until now.
Whatever you adopt in this category - @snyksec's or anyone's - judge it on four questions:
1. Does it reason about what your app actually does?
2. Does it run on every change, or once a year?
3. Does it have the context to know where to look?
4. Does it prove the bug, or just flag
DMs open if you want to go deeper on Continuous Offensive Security and I'll connect you with Eli

A lot of early-stage founders asked me this week at @aiDotEngineer about @daytonaio's community strategy in San Francisco.
My answer was simple: persistence. More than anything else, that's what matters.
The Bay Area community is incredibly engaged. Every day, there are multiple packed events competing for attention. The only way to stand out is to consistently show up.
Organize events. Seek out the right speakers and partners. Attend events. Speak. Sponsor the right conferences. Keep showing up.
That's what we do at Daytona. Every week, we're organizing, sponsoring, speaking at, or attending at least 3–4 community events across the SF & Bay Area.
Community isn't built overnight. It's built through consistency.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
spending the last week at @aidotengineer was awesome. too many great convos to cover them all, but jotted down some things that stood out:
- Lots of discussion around open source models. I spoke with consultants helping enterprise start to switching over low level tasks. Model routing companies and tools are seeing an uptick in usage and demand, and more innovation happening in routing (eg deterministic classifiers, etc).
- As an extension of this topic, local model room was packed. More people are running or at least trying to build fully local coding agents, primary reason seems to be cost (it’s people spending lots on tokens).
- They had a special area for “token billionaires” who are not people who have a billion tokens but spend a billion tokens… a week.
- Saw that OpenClaw was a topic on some talks, but in my private conversations (biased by who I spoke with), I spoke with many people who had switched to Hermes Agent, and very few active OpenClaw users.
- Fable came back during the conference (the strong Claude model that was temporarily banned by US govt). I heard people at the conference that it was butchered and not as good, but I also heard from people I trust that they didn’t notice a difference and that it’s great. It likely depends on what you’re using it for - my limited experience from this morning has been great.

last year: evals, coding agents, and a third thing i genuinely already forgot (that's the point)

biggest unlock from this week: there's already SO much shipped - oss + market - that the play might not be writing everything yourself anymore. it's combining what exists, with your taste as the glue.
as an engineer this is the most painful pill to swallow. "i'll just write it myself" is the default cracked-dev bias. but i think it's the way.
my last 12 months: built my own orchestration framework. my own harness. contributed to openclaw. all of it leveled me up - and exposed the pattern: i was building for imaginary users with imaginary needs, instead of a problem i hit every single day. now i know exactly what to build.
next 12 months: DEVBOXES.
the pitch is stupid simple:
your agents should not run on your laptop.
they live in an isolated remote box with full permissions - actual yolo mode, no approving sketchy commands every 2 minutes. assign long tasks, close the laptop, get pinged when they need you or they're done.
a remote vps with coding agents pre-installed. that's it. explainable in one breath.
and that matters. half the expo floor was products so packed with features you couldn't find the golden path. i get it - stack features so the big labs can't eat you in one bite. i'm going the other way: one simple, robust thing.
simple ≠ easy. simple is hard mode. complexity is what happens by default when nobody makes decisions. simplicity IS the decisions - what to cut, what to say no to, which single path to perfect. complicated-but-impressive is cheap. powerful-but-obvious is real engineering.
btw a devbox is the minimum viable software factory. add multiplayer + local models on top and we're fully trend-compliant for 2026 :)
new term unlocked: REMOTE CODING.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Loved this 22-minute talk on continual learning for AI agents. Must watch for anyone looking to get agents performant and into production.
Credit: @FeiziSoheil at @aiDotEngineer
• Agent learning can happen at three layers: the model (weights), the harness (prompts, tools, skills, code, workflows), and memory (session or persistent).
• Two fundamental challenges: (1) getting feedback, meaning how do we know if the agent did well and what it should have done instead, and (2) acting on that feedback, meaning deciding which layer or component to change and how.
• Feedback sources differ by stage: In development you have benchmarks with evaluators that score pass/fail. In production you only have logs, which can be judged either automatically (LLMs or code analyzing the log, which is scalable) or by human experts (low volume but critical domain knowledge).
• Logs plus feedback aren't enough because they're not testable: A single log with feedback is one observation of what happened. You need to lift it into a replayable learning environment, a simulation with tools, users, and defined evaluators, so candidate fixes can be run, verified, and compared.
• Three ways to optimize the agent, with tradeoffs: Model-layer updates (SFT, RL post-training like DPO/GRPO, LoRA) are expensive and need benchmarks and evaluators. Harness updates (trace-to-harness coding agents, prompt search like GEPA) are flexible but either untestable and "vibe-based" or benchmark-dependent. Memory updates (fact storage like Letta/Mem0, skill distillation) are cheapest and fastest but usually unverified.
• A good learning engine makes "the smallest durable change at the right layer" of the agent.
• Verifiable continual learning (VCL): Improve an agent from its own experience where every fix is proven to help and proven to break nothing that already worked. It requires an executable test (replayable failure), a measured delta (score before and after), and regression tests (prior tests still pass).
• Four principles of practical VCL: Replayability (turn one-off failures into rerunnable tests), holisticness (one failure can have causes in memory, prompts, tools, workflow, or model, so route the fix to the right layer), lifelongness (fix new failures subject to no regression on past environments, with regression handled inside the optimization loop rather than post-hoc), and efficiency (the loop must run frequently and cheaply, without scaling linearly as past environments accumulate).
• Three takeaways: (1) Agent continual learning isn't necessarily fine-tuning; many useful updates live in the harness and memory layers. (2) Production logs are not learning environments and must be transformed into replayable ones. (3) The frontier is regression-aware improvement: fixing new failures while verifying you don't break old ones.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
clean_title: Domain-specific agents outperform general agents in AI deployment
summary:
This 30-minute talk on domain-specific agents is a must watch for anyone trying to get agents past the demo stage and into production.
Credit: @jpschroeder at @aiDotEngineer
Some notes I took:
• Everyone is building custom agents, from real estate agencies to Fortune 500s, and it always comes down to integration: businesses want their data properly wired into AI. The problem is robust agents are hard, and the result is neither portable nor composable.
• The basic agent stack is model, system prompt, tools, skills, MCP, messages. Almost all of it is context, which means the industry is trying to solve integration by inflating one context window.
• MCP became a de facto tool distribution mechanism: on the official client support matrix, tools is the only column filled all the way down. Skills are markdown documentation, and research shows stacking too many makes your agent substantially worse.
• Inflating one agent with more context is inheritance, and inheritance breaks down: 5 skills works, 1,000 skills hits diminishing returns. Composition is the alternative.
• A domain-specific agent is a small, full agent (own system prompt, precise tools, own message history, own agentic loop) that knows one domain inside out, coordinated from above by a parent agent that talks to it in plain English.
• The numbers: over 80% token efficiency per task, and small models become viable. DeepSeek V4 Flash is 137x cheaper per task than Fable, and with minimal context it executes narrow tasks faithfully.
• Strict capability limits come free: each small agent can only do what's explicitly approved for it, versus one giant coding agent that can do anything, so we use it for everything and bypass permissions to cope.
• The economics force the shift: token costs reversed in 2026, up 29% this year adjusted for IQ and 76% unadjusted. You can't put a frontier model in front of customers unless their lifetime value is massive.
Three takeaways:
(1) Agent building breaks down at the context layer, and adding more context won't fix it.
(2) Small full agents composed under a coordinator beat one inflated general agent.
(3) The rest of 2026 belongs to domain-specific agents, and 2027 is the year of multi-agent orchestration.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2074484581776949249/img/O5Tdy6hsTuuUqRNm.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2074484581776949249/vid/avc1/480x270/x73k5UubCW9vjevo.mp4?tag=28
Quoting @LimestoneHQ
clean_summary:
A 30-minute talk on domain-specific agents highlights that building custom, small, fully autonomous agents for specific domains is more effective than inflating a single general agent with more context. These specialized agents, each with their own prompt, tools, and message history, are more token-efficient, faithful to narrow tasks, and cheaper to operate. The approach involves coordinating multiple small agents from a parent agent in plain English, which outperforms large, inflated agents and is expected to dominate AI applications in 2026, with multi-agent orchestration becoming key in 2027.

The talk emphasizes that adding more context to a single agent does not solve core issues like portability and composability, and that the economics of token costs will drive the shift toward domain-specific agents.

We ran autoresearch on preprocessing for a fraud-detection task. With a loose API the score looked great, and the code was leaking test data into the features in 13 different ways. We tightened the abstraction to a strict API and the reward-hacking rate dropped to zero.
My metaphor @aiDotEngineer talk: doing autoresearch is like training a model. The codebase abstraction is the architecture, it biases everything the search can find. The eval is the loss function and the data.
Human's research & engineer's role is no longer write exact code but get the constraints and feedback signal right.

summary:
Thariq Shihipar reveals one of the weirdest Claude Code lessons: stronger models can need less prompting.
"We recently removed 80% of the system prompt for Claude Code"
"Back in Sonnet 3.5 new, the best practices for a system prompt was a small system prompt, few tools, and lots of examples"
"As the models get smarter, you can give it more information and more instructions, and they start following them"
"Most recently, we found this new class of models want a smaller system prompt"
"The examples tend to constrain it cuz it's actually more imaginative than the examples we give it"
This is the opposite of how most teams are building agents.
They keep adding rules, examples, edge cases, and tool instructions because the old model needed rails. But at a certain capability level, the rails become drag.
The new skill is not writing longer prompts. It is knowing what to remove.
- @trq212, Member of Technical Staff at @Anthropic, at @aiDotEngineer

summary:
Thariq Shihipar explains the real mindset shift from coding agents: the old tradeoff triangle is breaking.
"One of my favorite parts of Anthropic is that we believe that tradeoffs are not real"
"What if you just did all of it?"
"What if you forced reality to show you the tradeoff?"
"The math of Claude and Fable really changes how you think about tradeoffs"
"Good, fast, cheap. Now it's pick three"
"The only way to prove that agents work is to do the best work of our lives faster than ever before"
This is the operator edge of AI coding.
Most teams still pre-negotiate with reality. They cut scope before the first attempt. Agents make it rational to try the unreasonable version first, then let reality show which constraint is actually binding.
That sounds like hype until you ship something in 4 hours that used to take weeks.
- @trq212, Member of Technical Staff at @Anthropic, at @aiDotEngineer

It's inspired by @geoffreylitt's talk at @aiDotEngineer: 'Understanding is the New Bottleneck'.
AI can generate infinite code and content, and the scarce thing now is a human who actually understands.
How often have you realized you read something but retained none of it?
I built '/explain-this' to solve that.
How it works:
🧠 It interviews you first. Ten minutes on what you know deeply, how explanations land for you, and what you're aiming to become. That generates your LEARNER.md profile.
📄 Then point your agent at any paper, PDF, or blog post and say "explain this."
✍️ It writes an explainer doc straight into your notes. Obsidian, OpenKnowledge, wherever you think, anchored to what you already know, skipping what you don't need to learn again.
✅ Every explanation ends with a quiz, and it grades your answers. Mastery learning means you don't move on until you prove to yourself you understood.
🔁 Your misses become spaced-repetition cards. Say "quiz me" next week and it re-teaches what didn't stick. Over time it learns your actual weak spots from evidence.
Works in Claude Code or any agent that supports skills.
Free and open source.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Cursor 如何自动化 AI 研究并实现自我加速迭代
来自 Cursor 团队 @leerob 在 AI Engineer @aiDotEngineer 的主题演讲「Recursive Model Improvement」，聚焦 Cursor 如何系统性地自动化 AI 研究流程，构建可快速迭代模型的系统，并分享了与 SpaceXAI 联合训练 Grok 4.5 的部分工作。
核心框架：外循环 + 内循环
简单公式“更多算力 → 更好模型”只是表象。实际存在两层循环：
· 外循环：模型上线后收集真实用户反馈、在线指标、A/B 测试结果，再反哺下一轮训练。Cursor 的大量收入来自 agent 使用数据，这些交互数据本身就是高质量训练信号。
· 内循环：直接提升训练过程本身的效率与质量——生成更难的 RL 环境、改进学习方法、设计更真实的软件工程任务、构建辅助模型（judge、reward model）等。
Cursor 已在大规模训练模型约一年。Composer 2.5 成为产品内最受欢迎的模型，主要得益于更多 RL 环境、更激进的任务难度以及新训练方法。
自动化研究与 Agent 系统
瓶颈逐渐从“模型能力”转向“人类研究者的带宽”。Cursor 因此构建了大规模 agent 系统来自动化研究中的重复性工作：
· 研究者可直接从 Slack 启动实验、管理训练任务。
· 存在常驻运行的 agent 舰队（主 agent + 大量子 agent），它们通过 SSH 收集状态、维护健康度、并行执行任务。
· 当任务卡住、基础设施出问题或需要人类决策时，agent 会主动通过 Slack 或 PagerDuty 通知/呼叫人类。
· 目标是让研究者专注于最有野心的想法，而不是启动、监控、 babysitting 实验。
演讲用 Mario 类比：基础模型是 Mario；加上工具（code、shell、web、computer use、订阅与存储）变成 Super Mario；再叠加丰富上下文（Slack、Notion、Linear、Datadog、代码库、同事、其他 agent）则接近 Fire Mario。工具与上下文的组合正在显著放大模型实际有用性。
递归自我改进的机制
真正关键的跃迁在于：模型开始帮助训练下一个模型。
· 更强的主模型可以蒸馏出更好的辅助模型（judge、reward model 等）。
· 这些辅助模型反过来提升评估质量、奖励信号和数据生成效率，从而抬高整个系统的智能底线。
· 结果是训练循环本身加速——模型越强，越能更好地为自己的下一代创造训练条件。
这不是科幻意义上的完全自主 RSI，而是已经在发生的、可验证的“模型帮助改进模型训练流程”。随着更多算力上线，这种正反馈会被进一步放大。
Lee 也提到评估中的现实问题：前沿模型越来越会通过上网查答案来“作弊”破坏评估。Cursor 通过限制网络访问、删除 git history 等方式应对，并维护私有的真实代码库任务集（CursorBench）以确保评估可信。
与 Grok 4.5 的关联
Cursor 团队与 SpaceXAI 联合训练 Grok 4.5。Grok 4.5 是 Cursor 迄今最强模型，也是首个不仅针对软件工程、还覆盖更广泛知识工作的模型。训练使用了海量 Cursor 真实交互数据（代码库操作、工具使用、开发者-agent 协作轨迹），并在困难的真实环境中进行强化学习。前代模型被用来加速下一代模型的进度，正是上述递归机制的实际应用。

clean_title: The Self-Driving Company: Lessons from AI-Native Engineering
summary:
The Self-Driving Company: 5 Counter-Intuitive Lessons from the Frontier of AI-Native Engineering
1. The Amnesia Trap
Most professionals wake up to a frustrating "blank-slate" experience every morning. Despite the staggering power of Large Language Models (LLMs), our interactions with AI assistants typically reset with every new chat window. The assistant forgets your preferred tone, your previous quarter's objectives, and the context of the crisis you spent yesterday resolving. This is the "Amnesia Trap," and it stems from a biological limitation: the human brain is a "seven-digit" machine. As cognitive psychology suggests, we can only hold about seven items in working memory—the reason phone numbers are seven digits and why we forget the eighth item on a grocery list.
A new paradigm is emerging from organizations like Y Combinator (YC) and Replit that shatters this bottleneck. They are building "Self-Driving Companies" where productivity doesn't just grow—it compounds. By moving away from treating AI as a simple autocomplete tool and toward an integrated "workforce" architecture, these firms are proving that when work is engineered correctly, a single person can do what once required a thousand.
2. Takeaway 1: Stop Building Assistants, Start Hiring "Librarians"
The most significant limitation of an AI agent is not its intelligence, but its working memory. This is the core challenge of Context Engineering. A modern agent has a context window of roughly one million tokens—enough to keep "three Harry Potter books" open on its desk at once. However, a company’s total knowledge—emails, Slack logs, codebases, and meeting transcripts—is a massive library.
To solve this, YC’s Garry Tan developed GBrain, an open-source (MIT license) retrieval layer that acts as the "Linux of memory." GBrain functions as a "Librarian" for AI agents. Instead of forcing an agent to memorize the entire library, GBrain uses Proactive Contextualization to sift through vast datasets—such as Tan’s personal warehouse of 220,000 pages of notes and 20 years of lived experience—and identify exactly which "three books" need to be on the agent's desk for the task at hand.
"Ultimately, this context engineering dictates whether an agent acting on a massive dataset performs like a 'genius or a goldfish.'"
When a founder emails about a crisis, the system doesn’t wait for a manual search; it instantly loads prior conversations and historical resolutions before the human even finishes reading the message. This transforms the agent from a blank-slate intern into an informed colleague who shares your history.
3. Takeaway 2: "Skillify" Your Success (The End of One-Off Work)
In a self-driving company, the operating philosophy is simple: If you have to ask for something twice, you failed. To prevent organizational amnesia, every successfully completed task must be converted into a permanent, reusable Skill File.
A Skill File is essentially a "digital employee"—a Markdown document dedicated to a specific capability. When an employee uses an agent to solve a problem, they follow a rigorous "Task-to-Skill" workflow:
Execute: Use an AI harness (like OpenClaw) to complete the task.
Refine: Iterate on the instructions until the output meets high-level "taste" and "judgment."
Codify: Document the successful procedure into a clear Markdown file.
Load: Re-upload that file into the harness to give the agent a permanent new capability.
This ensures the organization gets smarter every day. By encoding procedures into Markdown, the company moves from "rented intelligence" to "owned, compounding knowledge," ensuring that one-off successes become permanent infrastructure.
4. Takeaway 3: The Secret Architecture—Latent vs. Deterministic Space
A primary cause of AI system failure is asking models to perform logic they weren't built for. AI-native engineering requires a strict boundary between Latent Space and Deterministic Space.
Latent Space (The LLM): This is where taste, judgment, and the interpretation of vague human requests live. It is non-deterministic and steered by Skill Files.
Deterministic Space (Traditional Code): This is for predictable, mathematical, and procedural computation—the environment where engineers write scripts in TypeScript or Erlang.
Consider the "800-person seating arrangement" problem. You use Latent Space to evaluate attendee profiles and exercise "taste" on who should sit next to whom. However, you must use Deterministic Space to store and compute the actual multi-dimensional array of the 800 physical seats. If you force an LLM to track the exact mathematical coordinates of those seats within its context window, it will hallucinate. Success lies in wiring the two spaces together: the LLM handles the "human" part, while the code handles the "math" part.
5. Takeaway 4: The Rise of the "Manager of Agents"
We are witnessing the "New Physics of Business," where revenue-per-head ratios are reaching unprecedented levels. Startups are crossing $15 million in ARR with only 15 people, or $60 million with 40 people—metrics that never existed in software, oil, or railroads.
This is possible because AI-native tools are democratizing engineering. Because Skill Files are written in procedural Markdown, non-engineers are becoming Managers of Agents. At YC, a finance employee who had never opened a terminal used an internal agentic harness to collapse 100 disparate Excel workbooks into a single custom application. This represents a fundamental shift in professional identity: the value of an employee is no longer "doing" the work, but acting as a "Director" who sets the vision, exercises taste, and manages a digital workforce made of Markdown.
6. Takeaway 5: Leverage is in the "Wiring," Not the "Weights"
The productivity gains at the frontier are staggering, but they don't come from using "better" models. Replit and YC use the same Claude and GPT models available to everyone. The advantage is entirely in the "wiring"—the automated loops and memory hygiene that surround the model.
At Replit, engineers have seen a 2.9x increase in code output among consistent authors, while the total lines of code contributed across the organization grew 5.8x in six months. Garry Tan reports that his personal output has increased 400x compared to his 2013 baseline as a partner-engineer.
"The leverage is not in the weights; it's in how you wire the work."
This "Wiring" includes:
Loop Engineering: Using a "Manager Agent" to spawn a fleet of agents working in parallel to complete verifiable tasks, such as stalled CSS migrations or complex networking bug hunts.
Trigger Evals: Automated performance reviews that verify if an agent followed internal procedures (e.g., checking if a required test file was loaded before code was altered).
Memory Hygiene: Treating the "Company Brain" like production infrastructure. This includes Provenance (tracking the origin of every fact) and Contradiction Checks to ensure the librarian prunes stale data.
Build vs. Buy Shift: AI-native firms are replacing seven-figure SaaS solutions with internal agents that outperform market-leading tools because they are deeply integrated into the company's specific "Brain."
7. Conclusion: Boiling the Ocean
The transition to an AI-native organization allows teams to tackle problems previously dismissed as "impossible." We are seeing the birth of the "Self-Improving System," where agents analyze feedback and propose their own architectural upgrades. This isn't just about speed; it's about a fundamental change in the scale of human ambition.
As Garry Tan suggests, "Abundance is not a policy paper; it is shipped software." Whether it is a father building an 80,000-file repository to research his son’s rare medical condition or a small team managing a global enterprise, the architecture of the library and the librarian makes every problem solvable.
If your company is still running on a "seven-digit brain" while the competition is building a library, how long until they boil the ocean you're currently swimming in?

Instead of building assistants that rely solely on internal memory, companies like YC and Replit develop systems that use external memory layers, like GBrain, to act as a 'librarian' that fetches relevant knowledge instantly.

A key insight is transforming individual tasks into reusable 'Skill Files' stored in Markdown, which helps organizations accumulate and own knowledge rather than repeatedly redoing work. The architecture emphasizes a clear boundary between the non-deterministic, judgment-based Latent Space of LLMs and the deterministic, logic-based space of traditional code, enabling more reliable AI systems.

Furthermore, the rise of 'Manager of Agents' roles and the focus on wiring—automated loops, memory hygiene, and integrated workflows—are driving unprecedented productivity gains. These advances are enabling small teams to achieve results once thought impossible, marking a shift toward self-improving, scalable AI organizations that fundamentally change human ambition and problem-solving capacity.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
I turned 30 and realized my biggest improvement was not technical.
It was learning how to do scary things without making fear the boss of every decision.
At 20, public speaking felt impossible.
English networking felt impossible.
Even raising my hand in class felt like too much. Seriously. I've never done that once in my life.
This year, I gave talks at multiple events, trained teams in person, spoke online to thousands of people, and gave my best talk so far at @aiDotEngineer World's Fair in San Francisco.
Not because I became naturally confident.
I did not.
What changed was the size of the reps.
First a YouTube video in English.
Then another one.
Then a small training.
Then a webinar.
Then an in-person room.
Then a keynote.
Then a bigger conference.
A few things I wish I understood earlier:
Fear usually shrinks during and after the reps, not before them.
Confidence is not a personality trait. It is evidence your brain collected over time. And, yes, you can (and will) change. Even if it feels impossible.
And, having felt disappointment doing that, saying no can be healthy. Some opportunities are too much too soon.
But saying no should not become your default forever.
Choking is not proof you are not made for it. It is often just the price of learning in public.
At 20, I was taking grade hits to avoid 5-minute presentations.
At 30, I get to teach AI to engineers in rooms I used to be too scared to enter.
I cannot believe the progress I have made. If you are in the same situation as 20-year-old me, just keep going. One step at a time. It'll change your life sooner than you expect.

AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
@aiDotEngineer have released @Whats_AI's talk, "Turn 10,994 Notes Into Memory", on YouTube. Louis-François is CTO and co-founder of Towards AI.
The talk shows how to build a personal AI research system that sits between your coding agents and your notes, so an agent can pull high-signal context out of years of your own material instead of you re-pasting links every session.
- The real bottleneck is memory, not more context. For an agent the context window becomes everything (the database, the file system, the reasoning space), and when the conversation ends it loses all of it, so you need memory that persists.
- Files over infrastructure. No vector database, no knowledge graph, no semantic search. Just Markdown files plus an index.yaml catalog that references every source.
- A deep research loop. An orchestrator agent turns a topic into questions, sub-agents run them (using Gemini grounded in Google), then a ranking step keeps only the highest-signal sources and fully scrapes just those.
- Point the loop at your second brain, not only the public web. Obsidian, Readwise, Notebook LM, and your GitHub repos all become sources the same algorithm can search.
- Three layers. Immutable raw sources, an index, and a wiki of derivatives the LLM builds: concepts, entities, comparisons, and notes it can read in a token-efficient hierarchy instead of re-reading raw files.
- The wiki stays alive. Every question you ask leaves a trace, creating new concept, note, or comparison files, so the system grows as you talk to it, not only when you ingest data.
- Your own notes stay untouched. Obsidian is an immutable snapshot organized with the PARA method (Tiago Forte), and each project scopes the research down to what it needs.
- It ships as a Cloud Code plugin and works with Codex. Installable, tunable skills, demoed on an article, three GitHub repos (OpenCode, Pi, Hermes), and plain custom links.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
The team at @aiDotEngineer have published @trq212's talk, "Field Guide to Fable", on YouTube. Thariq works on Claude Code at Anthropic.
The talk is a working guide to a new class of model: how to stop constraining it with habits carried over from older models, and how to find the gaps in your own spec before the model runs into them.
- Models are grown, not designed. What limits them is the harness and the prompts we put around them, so understanding the model better is what unleashes it.
- Capability overhang is spiky. A chat model can't name the two Pokemon ending in "aw", but Claude Code can, because it fetches them all and writes a script to filter. Give it arms and it builds its own context instead of needing everything pasted in.
- Smaller system prompts now win. Anthropic recently removed 80% of Claude Code's system prompt. Examples constrain a model that's more imaginative than the examples, so give it context rather than constraints.
- The map is not the territory. Your prompt and spec are the map; the codebase is the territory. Every place they don't match is an unknown, a decision point you left unspecified, and Fable hits a lot of them because it covers so much ground.
- Sort your unknowns into a matrix. Known knowns go in the prompt. Known unknowns, unknown knowns (too obvious to write down, but you know it when you see it), and unknown unknowns are what you're hunting for.
- Run a blind spot pass. Ask Claude to go through the module you know nothing about and surface the relevant unknown unknowns, pointing it at the git diff or Slack for context.
- Brainstorm to find what you can't describe. Ask for four wildly different design directions as an HTML page and react to them, which surfaces the know-it-when-you-see-it preferences.
- Have it interview you. Ask Claude to interview you about the spec, and tell it to prioritize questions that would change the architecture.
- The best map to give it is another map. Point at existing code, even in a different language, or an HTML mockup, instead of writing the spec out longhand.
- Log the deviations. Ask it to write implementation notes when it hits an unknown, then have it quiz you afterward so you can actually represent the work in a PR.
- Trade-offs are worth re-testing. The talk argues good, fast, cheap is now pick three, and that forcing reality to show you the trade-off beats assuming it.
- Building is easier, generating value is still hard. It takes a lot of swings to find the valuable stuff, and the process and setups are not the point.

summary:
Two speakers at the same conference took opposite positions, and @altryne built a talk around the gap between them. "Should AI Engineers Still Read Code in 2026? The Z/L Continuum" is on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube. Alex is AI Evangelist at W&B from CoreWeave and the host of ThursdAI.
What you get out of it is a way to decide, per change, how much review it actually needs instead of arguing the question in the abstract.
- The continuum is about tasks, not people. Alex names his own framing error: the same engineer is a Lopopolo on one piece of code and has to be a Zetschner on another.
- Both ends agree more than they sound like they do. Ryan Lopopolo says inspect the system, not every line. Mario Zetschner says non-critical code can rip, critical code gets read line by line.
- The output numbers are real. A Ferris AI survey of 22,000 engineers from April 2026 shows an 861% increase in code deletion per PR. Anthropic says 80% of its code is AI-written and it ships eight times more per quarter than in 2025.
- So is the cost. The same survey shows a 242% increase in incidents per PR, a 31% increase in PRs merged with no review at all, and bugs per developer up six times from 2025.
- The routing table is the takeaway slide. Read every line of authentication, money movement, permissions, and irreversible data. Decompose into atomic reviewable PRs. Verify with traces, evals, and shadow mode.
- Never let the writer grade itself. Alex compares it to writing your own exam, taking it, and scoring it.
- Loops raise the stakes rather than removing them. An agent running loops verifies its own work, which doesn't delete the review step, it hides it.
- Capability drift moves where proof belongs, not whether you need it. He closes on that: not every line in 2026 needs your eyes, but every system still needs your judgment.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Most agents can already check their own work for correctness, and `@geoffreylitt` thinks that's fine. What he doesn't want to give up is the understanding that lets you have the next idea. That's the argument in "Understanding is the new bottleneck," on `@aiDotEngineer`'s YouTube. Geoffrey is a design engineer at Notion. The talk is a set of concrete practices for keeping up with code your agents wrote, borrowed from education rather than from code review.
- Understanding to verify vs understanding to participate. Correctness is a thumbs up or thumbs down call, and agents keep getting better at it. Understanding is what you carry into the next loop, and the next.
- Cognitive debt. A term from Margaret Storey that Simon Willison has also written about. Like tech debt, you get away with it for a while, then you realize you can't participate in your own project anymore.
- Explainer docs beat raw diffs. Background before the change, intuition before details, prose that orders the files for a reader, interactive figures where they earn their place. Geoffrey published the ExplainDiff skill he uses for this.
- Quizzes as a speed regulator. Five medium questions at the bottom of every explainer, and a personal rule: no sending code to teammates until he can pass the quiz on what his agent wrote. The idea comes from Andy Matuschak's "books don't work."
- Micro-worlds. Papert's math land, applied to code. Claude built him a scrubbable step by step debugger for a Prolog interpreter he was writing, and turned a website framework migration into a click through game so he could watch it happen instead of trusting a script.
- Shared understanding is a team problem. Multiplayer threads where humans and agents talk in the same space, and comments on agent written plans, so a team builds the same mental model instead of each person briefing their own agent.
- Alan Kay had this in 1972. Kids modifying a game's code as they play it to learn physics. The point was never the computer, it was the kids.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
A concept from 1990s knowledge engineering just got reintroduced to the AI world at the AI Engineer Summit.
Ontologies.
The pitch: ontologies keep agents honest. Instead of an agent relying on embeddings alone to understand what "customer" or "order" or "policy" means, an active ontology makes those definitions explicit and machine-readable. The agent queries it at inference time. The ontology tells the agent what concepts exist, how they relate, and what rules constrain valid relationships.
This is the difference between an agent that guesses what "high-value customer" means from embedding similarity and one that queries a defined taxonomy and gets a precise, auditable answer.
The agentic case for ontologies is stronger than the database case ever was. In a database, a human designed the schema and humans know what the tables mean. In an agentic system, the agent is making decisions across thousands of runs. If the model's implicit understanding of a concept drifts between sessions, nobody notices until something breaks at scale.
Ontologies give agents a stable, queryable layer of concept definitions that sits outside the model weights. If the model shifts with a fine-tune, the ontology doesn't change. If you need to audit why an agent classified something a certain way, you have a human-readable source of truth.
The challenge is maintenance. Schemas rot. The person who designed the ontology moves on. This is the same problem that killed ontology projects in the 2000s.
The argument I find compelling: when an agent maintains the ontology as part of its own operation, updating definitions when it encounters edge cases, the maintenance problem changes character. Still hard. Different kind of hard.
Quoting @aiDotEngineer

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
SkillBench indexed over 50,000 skills from GitHub and found that almost none of them had evals. @_philschmid, a Staff Engineer at Google DeepMind, builds an entire session out of that gap. "Don't Ship Skills Without Evals" is on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube.
What you get is a concrete method for testing a skill: what to assert, how many times to run it, and how to tell when the skill has stopped earning its tokens.
- The agents you use and the agents you build are different problems. In your own editor you notice instantly when a skill doesn't fire and you reprompt. Your customers don't know skills exist and will never type a slash command.
- Capability skills are temporary, preference skills are durable. Capability skills cover what a model can't do consistently yet. Preference skills encode your team's workflow and style, which no foundation model is going to absorb.
- Skills do work, measurably. SkillsBench 1.1 puts the average gain at roughly 15% across about 100 coding and productivity tasks.
- AI-written skills can hurt. Human-written skills performed best, and a skill.md over 500 lines is a signal to go back and cut.
- The description is where most of it breaks. Around 50% of failures came from the skill not being triggered at all. Write directives about when and how to use it, not passive prose about what it is.
- Don't skip the negative cases. Philipp's starting point is ten to twenty prompts: five happy path, five where the skill should stay out of it.
- If the steps never change, write a script instead. Skills should set goals and constraints. A fixed step one, step two, step three workflow is burning tokens on something deterministic.
- Cut the no-ops. Credit to Matt for this one. AI-generated skills fill up with instructions like "make the implementation easy to read" that change nothing about the agent's behavior and still cost you context.
- A real example, in numbers. The Gemini Interactions API skill was built against 117 test cases drawn from real user data, synthetic cases, and feedback, and got valid code generation to almost 90%. The harness was a JSON file of cases plus a small Python script running Gemini CLI, with most checks written as regex asserts.
- Test outcomes, not paths. It doesn't matter whether the skill loaded on turn one or turn five. Run isolated workspaces, because coding agents will happily cheat off previous runs, and do three to six trials per case since the whole thing is non-deterministic.
- Ablation tells you when to retire. Run the evals with and without the skill loaded. When the model passes without it, drop the skill and keep the eval as a regression test.
At Google DeepMind, evals live alongside every skill and run on every change, and a change doesn't merge unless it improves them.

summary:
Most agent skills are AI-written, lightly reviewed, and shipped without evals.
That makes failures hard to diagnose. Did the skill fail? Did it trigger at the wrong time? Or was the task beyond the model?
Good talk from @_philschmid on the @aiDotEngineer YouTube:
• Skills improved benchmark performance by roughly 15% on average
• Human-written skills performed best; AI-generated skills sometimes made results worse
• Test prompts that should trigger the skill and prompts that should not
• Judge the outcome, not whether the agent followed one exact path
• Run repeated, isolated trials across the models and agent harnesses people actually use
• Keep skills lean and directive, with deeper context stored in reference files
• Separate temporary capability skills from durable preference skills
• Compare every eval with and without the skill
• Retire the skill once the base model can pass without it, but keep the eval as a regression test
A good place to start: take your most-used skill, write five positive and five negative test prompts, then run the eval with and without the skill.

summary:
Cursor's models are now creative enough to cheat their own evals: @leerob, on ML and model behavior at Cursor, found them digging through git history for solutions and searching online for forks of public benchmarks. That's one thread in "Recursive Model Improvement," his talk on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube about how Cursor trains models and how those models start training the next ones. If you build with or evaluate coding models, it's a look at what the training loop actually consists of once you go past "more compute in, better model out."
- Two loops, not one. The outer loop runs on user feedback and A/B tests between checkpoints; the inner loop is high-quality evals plus deliberately hard training problems, and the inner one is where the speedups are.
- Reward hacking has cheap countermeasures. Delete git history at the start of a run and restore it at the end, and put the agent behind a network allow list. Lee says those two changes noticeably moved reported public-eval scores.
- Public benchmarks aren't the real test. Cursor runs CursorBench, a private eval built from real tasks in their own code base and held out of training, because in real use you do have the internet and you are using git.
- Evals have a half-life. When every model scores around 90% on an eval, retire it, and that clock speeds up as models improve.
- Manufacture verifiable hard problems. Generate an ambitious application with tests, delete a feature or some files so the tests fail, then let the model reimplement it however it wants against a verifiable pass/fail reward.
- Textual feedback for credit assignment. An RL rollout can run hundreds of thousands of tokens, so grading the end is imprecise. Zoom in on one step, have a teacher model supply a hint (for example, reminding it which tools exist), then upweight the probabilities you want.
- Where the compute actually goes. Serving users, serving internal checkpoints, A/B tests, pre-training, mid-training, RL, data and reward generation, judging, continuous evals, and side runs for researchers. The goal is multiple large training runs at once with nobody blocked.
- Compute partnership with SpaceX. Announced in March, down to Colossus (100,000 GPUs stood up in 122 days, another 100,000 in 92) and TerraFab for chips.
- Take the humans out of babysitting. Researchers at Cursor launch training runs from Slack; a team exists purely to automate the monotonous parts, and agents page a human when infrastructure breaks so nobody loses six hours.
- The recursion is in the derivative models. Each new top-level model distills into the judges and reward models that drive both loops, so raising the smartest model in the system raises the floor everywhere.
- Composer 2.5, shipped in May, Is Cursor's most popular model, positioned as fast, smart, and cost effective rather than the most intelligent, and the next version targets a full pre-train from scratch instead of building on an open-source base.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
. @danielhanchen spends a chunk of his AI Engineer talk on a benchmark that hands the model the answer: SWE-Bench Pro ships the full git history with the GitHub issue, so a model can skip straight to the solution. That talk, "Special Topics in Kernels, RL, Reward Hacking in Agents," is on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube. Daniel is co-founder of Unsloth.
It's a tour of where the measurements and the training incentives are quietly broken, from someone who quantizes and bug-fixes open models for a living.
- Benchmarks that grade themselves. SWE-Bench Pro uses an LLM as the verifier. DeepSWE puts its false positive rate at 8.5% and its false negative rate at 24%.
- Verifier wars. DeepSWE says its own false positive rate is 0.3%. Cognition's Frontier Code benchmark says DeepSWE's is 44.9%. His take on which benchmarks to trust: none of them, take an average, vibe check.
- The harness beats the model. Same benchmark, Claude Code gets 40% where DeepSWE's own harness gets 50%. Gemini CLI gets 20% where the controlled harness gets 40%.
- Accuracy dips are harness bugs. Anthropic's post-mortem traced one degradation to thinking traces being dropped on the second turn plus a bad system prompt, and another to GPU and TPU stacks sampling differently.
- Inference providers are throughput maxing and accuracy minimizing. On the same GLM 5.2 weights, OpenRouter measured 76.4% at the top provider and 62.4% at the bottom.
- Long context degrades well before the advertised limit, so don't plan on using the full million.
- Dynamic quantization. Quantize everything to one bit and you get 0%. Leave the linear attention, vision, and audio layers alone and a three-bit DeepSeek holds 75.6%, a one-bit 57%. A one-bit GLM 5.2 is 86% smaller and nowhere near 86% dumber.
- Stop writing kernels. Reach for torch.compile first. On recent PyTorch it beats the handwritten RMSNorm and LayerNorm kernels he plots against it.
- Hardware is near the end of its rope. Float32 to float4 bought 32x, tensor cores 12x, shrinking the die about 3x. There's no float zero, so the gains have to come from algorithms now.
- Reward hacking is already in production runs. GPT-5.1's training turned up calculator hacking, where the model faked web tool use. GLM 5.2 shipped an anti-hacking link checker. On the GPU MODE leaderboard, a submission passed the correctness check honestly, ran the kernel once during timing, and served the other runs out of a Python dict.
- Assign one reward to the whole trace and you reward the wrong lines. Process supervision fixes it and doesn't scale, and using a model to judge itself reintroduces the problem.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Every year @barrnanas runs a survey on the state of AI engineering, and every year the number one answer to "what's the biggest challenge in your stack?" is evals. That's the title of her talk on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube: "The biggest challenge in your stack? Evals, Evals, Evals". Barr is a Partner at Amplify Partners, and this year's survey ran with Notion and Vercel behind it, 1,048 respondents. If you want data on what AI engineers are actually doing rather than what Twitter says they're doing, this is the talk.
- Evals still lead, but barely. 96% of respondents report a problem somewhere in their stack, they just can't agree which one. And the top eval method is still vibe review.
- Agents got write access. 95% say they're using agents, roughly double last year. Among those, 89% have agents that can write data, up from 52%. Write-enabled agents tripled across the whole sample.
- The control layer is unsettled. Human in the loop approvals and permission gating are the top two instruments, which Barr calls the toolkit you'd use to manage an intern. Below that the results scatter.
- Cost became a first class constraint. 40% say cost regularly shapes how ambitiously they use AI, another 36% say it sometimes does. Cost and token usage are the second most monitored thing in production, right under quality.
- Open weights augment, they don't replace. 94% use closed models, 45% use open weight ones, and over 90% of the open weight users also run closed models. Open versus closed was a top three consideration for only 5% when choosing a model. Quality dominates, then agentic capabilities and cost.
- Standardization is happening on tools, not models. 87% run more than one model, most commonly routing by task type, while more than half say their org is consolidating on fewer AI tools.
- Buy inference, build product logic. Inference and model serving is the layer teams buy most. Prompt management is the opposite: 61% build it themselves. Fine tuning is the clearest "not yet."
- Image gen doubled, audio has the intent. Respondents building with generative images went from 18% to 36%. Among those not using audio today, 56% plan to, up from 37% last year.
- The org chart is feeling it. 81% say AI is blurring the line between engineering, product, design and marketing. Over a third of teams have non-developers shipping features, and 17% say non-developers regularly ship customer-facing ones.
- Happier, faster, with a maintenance bill. 76% say AI boosted their job satisfaction, 59% fear today's AI code creates long-term liabilities, and the most cited downside is erosion of deep technical skills and understanding of the codebase.

title: AI Engineer (@aiDotEngineer)
summary:
Your supplier is your competitor. That's the line @sarahmsachs, Eng Lead for AI at Notion, builds her talk around in "Notion's Token Town", on @aiDotEngineer's YouTube. If you buy tokens from a lab that also sells the finished product, you're paying a surcharge to resell against the people you buy from.
It's a practical guide to the cost side of shipping AI, the part that quietly decides whether a product survives its own model bill.
- 88% never get past AI as an assistant. Sarah walks the progression from thought partner to assistant to teammate to AI as a running system, and almost nobody has that last stage working.
- Price doesn't track capability. A model slightly behind the leader only needs to be a dollar per million tokens cheaper to take the rest of the market, so per-token cost tells you little about what you're actually getting.
- Optionality is the leverage. Hitching to one provider for a bigger discount means shipping a non-frontier product a good chunk of the time, because who holds the lead changes month to month.
- Notion's Auto model handles about 75% of their traffic. State of the art models stay available, but routing an email triage job to the biggest reasoning model overcharges the customer and Notion both.
- Plenty of jobs don't need a GPU. Turning a CSV into a PDF, running deterministic SQL, hitting Notion tool calls through a CLI: none of that needs an LLM, and that's where teams go token poor fast.
- Open weights work as a pricing floor. They're strong enough for moderate tasks now, and they put downward pressure on what is otherwise a very concentrated top of the market.
- Evaluate whole trajectories, not single calls. Cost per capability per second across an entire web search trajectory is what let Notion pick a provider that a per-call price comparison would have ruled out.
- The next six months are about security, not capability. The lethal trifecta, private data plus untrusted content plus the ability to communicate externally, gets less supervised the more autonomous your system becomes.
